teile.name: Rewrite request
teile.text: Client request three just landed. Same guide, new tone, again. Claude Projects targets that nightmare. But what does it cost?
teile.szene: Black-haired presenter in black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses slumps at a cluttered desk at night, rubbing his forehead, medium shot, painted open-world-game poster style, warm lamp light, calm space above and below.

teile.name: Workspace
teile.text: Surprise: free accounts get projects, up to five. Each is a workspace with its own chats and knowledge base.
teile.szene: Presenter in black leather jacket and cyan glasses slides a stack of folders into a glowing cabinet in a neon-lit city office, medium shot, painted urban game-poster style, no readable text.

teile.name: Context
teile.text: Imagine uploading a client's brand notes. Claude uses them as background, like a coworker who actually opened the brief.
teile.szene: Hypothetical scene: a focused coworker in a painted urban studio leafs through a thick briefing folder while the cyan-glasses presenter looks on, impressed, medium shot, open-world-game poster style, golden light.

teile.name: Instructions
teile.text: But how does it know the tone? Add project instructions, like a formal tone or a specific role.
teile.szene: Presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses leans over a workbench, writing a plan with a pen while a thoughtful client figure watches, medium shot, painted game-poster style, soft rim light.

teile.name: Capacity
teile.text: Paid plans go further: when knowledge nears limits, Claude can stretch project capacity up to 10x. Pro includes projects.
teile.szene: Wide painted shot of a tall archive room where a worker adds an extension shelf as the old one fills up, presenter watching from the aisle, moody blue lighting.

teile.name: Honest limit
teile.text: Limit: usage counts against your plan, and income isn't promised. Still, that third rewrite now starts with context.
teile.szene: Presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses sits calmly at a tidy desk, nodding with a small smile as he reviews work, medium close shot, painted game-poster style, warm morning light.

teile.text: Be sure to like, share and save this video.

regeln: Within each spoken phase use multiple distinct relevant shots, roughly 3-5 seconds each for Shorts; long videos can allow purposeful longer demonstrations. Preserve continuous narration and accurate subtitle timing.
A zoom, crop, subtitle change or decorative background does not count as a new motif. Never fill missing images with candles, unrelated stock or background-only frames.
Show the main image prominently; avoid tiny repeated photos in a mostly empty vertical frame. Preserve genuine evidence and important image details.
For AI Tools Explained identify the exact tool briefly, then show genuine interface views and different source-supported examples. Never present stock or an illustration as a real tool result.
Use original urban painted open-world-game poster styling for fictional scenes and presenters; no copied game characters. Match narrated action and era.

Clear speech and readable captions alone do not make a professional video. Inspect useful motif changes and narration-image alignment over the entire video. Missing main imagery is a substantial defect.
Include mandatory spoken like, share and save calls at the correct format-specific positions. Do not replace this requirement with a different CTA.

AI Tools Explained is for viewers with a practical task. Do not read parameter counts, architecture names, pipeline tags, context lengths or benchmark claims as a substitute for useful explanation. Explain the human task, the source-supported action and a concrete limit. A generic trending-tools question failed story review twice; prefer a specific visual workflow.

The user confirmed original presenter references on 2026-10-05: Business Origin Stories uses the blue-eyed man with a fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch; AI Tools Explained uses the black-haired man with black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses. Preserve identity and typical clothing, vary action and setting.

Introduce the correct presenter at the opening and bring that same presenter back during the video in useful actions. Do not confine the figure to the ending. Do not replace original channel figures with different fictional people; anonymous period workers remain clearly illustrative supporting people, never a real-founder likeness.

Prefer vivid original painted open-world-game scenes to long holds on lifeless documentary photos. Preserve factual accuracy and show authentic tool examples briefly as evidence. Camera moves alone are not new motifs or full character animation.

The user confirmed on 2026-10-05 that both new delivered videos are much better than before. Preserve the original painted world, recurring channel identity, matching main imagery, music and useful scene changes. The long-term quality target remains 10/10; the user did not give these videos a numeric score. Do not replace their actual AI scores or the existing 7/10 delivery threshold with the aspirational target.

Verify every tool claim, UI view, and example against source material; never invent technical capabilities or user examples.
Show authentic interface screenshots or genuine tool output for each spoken element; avoid unrelated stock, metaphors, or filler images.
Identify the specific AI tool and the practical human task it solves within the first 3 seconds of the video.
Keep the main image prominent; avoid tiny filler shots, empty vertical frames, or unrelated background‑only frames.
Sync narration, subtitles, and visual motif changes precisely; each technical term must appear on screen as it is spoken.
Use original urban painted open‑world‑game styling for fictional scenes; do not copy characters from games or other media.
Include a single natural “like, share, and save” call‑to‑action placed appropriately within the narrative flow.
Focus on human‑centric, task‑oriented language; omit architecture names, benchmark numbers, and low‑level menu details.
Treat reviewer feedback as provisional data; do not infer unobserved causes or make absolute claims about retention or view counts.
Ensure every script passes a complete validation checklist (fact‑check, script notes, internal ratings) before production.

belege.text:
Official Anthropic Claude documentation/help page (https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9517075-what-are-projects).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
What are projects? | Claude Help Center
Note: A new version of projects is now available in beta, rolling out in stages starting with Claude Code. We've started moving existing projects for some Pro and Max users to the new version. See The new version of projects (beta) below.
Projects allow you to create self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases. Within each project, you can upload documents, provide context, and have focused chats with Claude.
Projects are available to all users, including those with free Claude accounts. Free users can create a maximum of five projects.
The new version of projects (beta)
We're rolling out a new version of projects in stages, starting with Claude Code. In the new version, a project is one conversation: you say what you need as it comes to you, and Claude breaks the work into parallel threads that run in the cloud. Claude tells you what's done and what's waiting on you, and if you close your laptop, the threads keep going. Every thread starts with the project's files, repositories, instructions, and memory, and the project's Library collects the files you add and the files Claude produces.
The new version is now available in beta to select Pro and Max subscribers who use Claude Code, and to some Pro and Max users whose existing projects we’ve moved to the new version. If you have it, you'll see "Projects" in the sidebar at claude.ai/code and in the Code tab of the Claude desktop app. More Claude Code users on Pro and Max plans will get access as the rollout expands, and chat, Cowork, Team, and Enterprise will follow. If you're on Pro or Max and don't have access yet, you can join the waitlist .
We’ve started moving existing projects for some Pro and Max users to the new version. Nothing is lost or deleted in the move. Everything in your project comes with it: your instructions, files, full chat history, and scheduled tasks. You’ll pick up right where you left off. If you've used an existing project within the last 30 days, we’ll email you before we move your projects. Other existing projects in chat and Cowork stay on the current version for now, and we’ll move them as the rollout expands.
Projects draw from your plan's usage like any other use of Claude, and running several threads at once uses it faster.
For more on the new version, see Projects in the Claude Code docs. The rest of this article describes the current version of projects.
A key benefit of projects is the ability to provide context for your chats with Claude. You can upload relevant documents, text, code, or other files to a project's knowledge base, which Claude will use to better understand the context and background for your individual chats within that project.
In addition, you can define project instructions for each project to further tailor Claude's responses. For example, instructing Claude to use a more formal tone or answer questions from the perspective of a specific role or industry.
Enhanced project knowledge with RAG is only available to users with paid Claude plans (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise).
When using a paid plan, your projects automatically scale to handle large amounts of content through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). When your project knowledge approaches context limits, Claude seamlessly enables RAG mode to expand capacity by up to 10x while maintaining response quality.
For more information on leveraging expanded project knowledge capacity, see Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) for projects .
Collaboration and sharing (Team and Enterprise plans only)
For users on Team and Enterprise plans, projects can be shared with other members of your organization, enabling powerful collaboration and knowledge sharing capabilities. The sharing system includes:
Can view: Members can see project contents, knowledge, and instructions, and chat within the project, but cannot edit it.
Can edit: Members can modify project instructions and knowledge, add/remove members, update member settings, and actively contribute to the project.
Share to specific members instead of making a project fully private or public to the entire organization.
Make a previously-created private project visible to the whole organization.
Individual sharing: Share projects with specific team members by email.
Bulk sharing: Add multiple users at once using email lists.
Organization-wide sharing: Make projects available to everyone in your organization either when creating the project or afterward.
Note: If an Owner or Primary Owner disables public projects, organization-wide sharing will be disabled both when creating the project and afterward.
Admin controls: Owners can turn off project sharing for your organization, or on Enterprise plans for specific roles. Turning off Share projects also turns off Public projects . When sharing is off, users can't share projects with new users or groups, and existing shares stay in place.
Shared with me tab: Easily find projects that others have shared with you.
Email notifications: Get notified when someone shares a project with you.
Access management: Project creators can modify permissions or remove access as needed.
Multiple members can contribute documents, create chats, and work together within the same project environment, making projects ideal for team collaboration.
For more information on getting started with projects, see How can I create and manage projects?
For more information on private projects and visibility settings on Team and Enterprise plans, see Project visibility and sharing .

This guide assumes that you have:
A clear definition of the success criteria for your use case
Some ways to empirically test against those criteria
A first draft prompt you want to improve
If not, spend time establishing that first. See Define success criteria and build evaluations for tips and guidance.
Don’t have a first draft prompt? Generate one with the metaprompt recipe from the Claude Cookbook.
For model-specific tuning guidance for Claude’s latest models, start here.
This guide focuses on success criteria that are controllable through prompt engineering.
Not every success criterion or failing eval is best solved by prompt engineering. For example, you can sometimes improve latency and cost more easily by choosing a different model.
All prompting techniques (from clarity and examples to XML structuring, role prompting, thinking, and prompt chaining) are covered in Prompting best practices . That’s the living reference; start there.
For general prompt engineering craft beyond Claude-specific techniques, see the blog post on best practices for prompt engineering .
If you’re an interactive learner, you can start with the interactive tutorials instead!
